common_name: Simba Dwarf Umbrella Bamboo (Compact Non-Invasive Clumper)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in partial shade in moist, fertile, well-drained soil; Simba's compact ultimate size makes it well suited to large containers, foundation beds, and small gardens where standard umbrella bamboo would outgrow the space.

directions: Simba is a genuinely dwarf selection of umbrella bamboo, reaching only about a third the height of the species while keeping the same dense, arching, fountain-like habit and fine, narrow leaves. Like all Fargesia, it forms a tight, non-running clump with pachymorph rhizomes and never spreads into lawns or neighboring beds, so it needs no root barrier even in a small yard. It tolerates more sun and wind than most Fargesia once established but still colors and performs best with some afternoon shade and consistently moist soil. Its restrained scale makes it one of the better bamboos for edging a path, screening a patio corner, or long-term container culture on a deck or balcony.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in partial shade to full sun in moist, well-drained soil with some shelter from drying wind; site where the narrow, purple-flushed foliage can be viewed up close.

directions: Nymphenburg is a German-raised selection of Chinese fountain bamboo grown for its slender, narrow leaves flushed with purple and its densely arching, fountain-form habit. Like the species it forms a tight, well-behaved clump that never runs by rhizome, so it can be planted safely near property lines, patios, or mixed borders without a containment barrier. It takes more sun than typical F. nitida selections without leaf scorch, though color and vigor are best with a sheltered site and protection from harsh afternoon sun in hot climates. Established clumps make a dense, elegant privacy screen or specimen planting and need little more than an annual mulch and consistent moisture to thrive.

common_name: Campbell Robusta Bamboo (Large Clumping Bamboo with White Sheaths)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in partial shade in moist, fertile, well-drained soil; give it room to develop its full upright stature and shelter from hot, direct afternoon sun in warmer zones.

directions: Campbell is a fast-growing, large-statured selection of Fargesia robusta with tall, slender, deep-green culms wrapped in pale, near-white culm sheaths that persist into early summer, giving new groves a striking bicolor look. It is more sun-tolerant than most Fargesia, with sturdy leaves that hold up without curling in brighter light, though it still performs best and stays lushest with afternoon shade and reliably moist soil. Like all Fargesia it spreads by tight pachymorph rhizomes and never runs, so it can be used as an unrestrained privacy screen or specimen even in a modest-sized garden. Its rapid growth and substantial mature height make it one of the quickest Fargesia selections to establish a dense screen.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; install a deep rhizome barrier before planting, since this running bamboo spreads more slowly than most Phyllostachys but is not truly contained without one.

directions: Boryana, also called leopard or tiger bamboo, produces culms that emerge plain green and develop an irregular pattern of dark brown to blackish blotches over their first two to three growing seasons, eventually resembling mottled snakeskin rather than the solid black of straight-species nigra. Among the Phyllostachys, it is regarded as one of the slower and more restrained spreaders, though a rhizome barrier is still recommended for reliable long-term containment in any but the most cold-limited sites. It is exceptionally cold hardy for a large timber-type bamboo, tolerating temperatures near 0°F once established, and the tall, upright culms make an excellent screen or grove planting. Thin older culms selectively each year to keep the mottled pattern of younger canes visible and to maintain good light and air movement through the grove.

planting.note: Plant container-grown divisions in spring in moist to wet, fertile, well-drained-to-poorly-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; install a 30-mil rhizome barrier 24–36 inches deep before planting, since this is still a spreading running bamboo despite its comparatively contained reputation.

directions: Incense bamboo takes its name from the mild, sweet, sandalwood-like fragrance released by its culms and wine-colored culm sheaths in warm weather, a distinctive feature among hardy running bamboos. Its rhizomes and roots carry air channels that let it thrive in consistently wet or poorly drained soil where most Phyllostachys struggle, making it a good choice for a low spot, pond margin, or rain garden edge that still needs a tall screening plant. The perpendicular branching habit builds a dense, layered canopy that blocks wind and sightlines effectively, and the abundant spring shoots are considered among the best-tasting of any temperate bamboo, whether eaten raw or cooked. It spreads by rhizome like other Phyllostachys and still requires a barrier for reliable long-term containment, though gardeners and growers commonly describe it as comparatively easier to manage than the most aggressive running species.

common_name: Aureocaulis Bamboo (Solid Gold-Culm Yellow Groove Bamboo)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun for the richest culm color; install a deep rhizome barrier before planting since this is a running bamboo.

directions: Aureocaulis is the solid-gold-culm form of yellow groove bamboo, ripening from bright yellow to deep golden yellow with only an occasional faint green pinstripe, unlike the boldly green-striped 'Spectabilis' selection of the same species. Strong spring sun can flush young culms with a temporary red blush that fades to gold over the first season, adding extra seasonal interest to new growth. It shares the species' exceptional cold hardiness, tolerating temperatures near –20°F once established, making it one of the few reliably yellow-culmed bamboos suited to genuinely cold northern gardens. Like all Phyllostachys it runs aggressively by rhizome and must be planted within a deep barrier or managed with annual trenching; full sun and an open, uncrowded planting site bring out the best culm color.
